title: Request timeline investigation — Console demo (Conversio)
redwood_attendees: Jordan Reyes (Customer Success Engineer - joining briefly)
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Conversio through the Console request timeline and debugging flows. Key topics: request trace correlation, error classification, KV cache fallbacks, role-based access for logs, and an ask to run an import of 48h of sample traces for a follow-up benchmark. Conversio raised security/residency and latency/cost tradeoffs; next steps agreed include a pilot test, security docs share, and a joint runbook creation.
action_items: Samir to send security whitepaper and SOC2 summary by 2025-07-02
Maya to provision sandbox tenant and upload console demo guide link by 2025-07-03
Lena to share 48h sample request IDs and spike dataset by 2025-07-06
Team to schedule pilot kickoff (30m) week of 2025-07-07
next_steps: Security docs and SOC2 pack shared
Upload sample traces to sandbox and run baseline traces
Follow-up deep-dive on observability SLOs and cost tuning
transcript:
[00:00] Samir (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. This is Samir from Redwood Inference — with me is Maya, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Marco (Conversio - CTO): Good, thanks. Quick intro: I'm Marco, CT O, and running infra. Lena and Ravi are on for ML and SRE.
[00:13] Lena (Conversio - Head of ML): Hi all. We want to see how we can triage user-facing hallucination incidents and slow token generation — mostly using the console.
[00:20] Maya (Redwood SE): Great, we'll focus on the request timeline view, how to jump from a failing request to logs, model variant fallbacks, and the KV cache behavior — and we'll show how audit logs and RBAC surface sensitive data.
[00:29] Ravi (Conversio - SRE): Quick FYI — our stack is k8s EKS, we run a mix of hosted endpoints and a few dedicated instances. Data residency is EU-first, and we need KMS integration for any private deployments.
[00:38] Samir: Noted. We'll call out where VPC/private differs from hosted. Ok, opening the Console — bear with me, my demo tenant is a sandbox so names might be generic.
[00:47] Maya: Jumping to the Request Timeline. This is the main timeline for a single inference request. You can see the client call, routing, model execution, any cache hits, and the final response.
[00:57] [01:00] (soft typing in background)
[01:05] Maya: Here we've got a sample request that had a long tail. See the spike at the model execution step — if you click that, you get the kernel-level timings and the per-layer latency.
[01:15] Lena: Are those timings actual GPU kernels or synthetic estimates?
[01:19] Maya: They're sampled from the runtime and include kernel execution plus serialization. They can be noisy. We also show the host-side queue time. Important note: for quantized runs the kernel selection changes and you'll see different stage durations — sometimes the HVX path, sometimes int8.
[01:34] Ravi: We saw an incident where a subset of requests tripped a fallback to a smaller model and still returned 500s. How would I trace that?
[01:41] Maya: Good question. In the timeline you can expand the routing block — it lists policy decisions. In that case you'll see a fallback event with a reason: e.g., "resource_exhausted" or "timeout". You can click the fallback event and it surfaces both the original model attempt, the fallback variant used, and the server-side stderr/stdout snippets for that exec.
[01:58] Samir: Also we correlate request IDs across the fronting API and the serving runtime, so you can jump directly to the KV cache diagnostic if there was a cache miss that caused extra work.
[02:09] [02:10] Marco: Is the KV cache per-tenant or per-model? Sometimes we saw cache poisoning between experiments.
[02:16] Maya: Cache granularity is per-tenant and per-model version. We isolate namespaces in Dedicated/Private. In hosted, we still shard KV by tenant ID. But there's a race when rolling model versions — cache keys include model version hash to avoid cross-version contamination.
[02:32] Lena: That's good. Can we also see the prompt and any redacted PII? We need to know what context triggered the hallucination without exposing PHI.
[02:40] Maya: Yes — by default sensitive fields are redacted in the UI; you can request a redaction escalation in the audit trail. If you have Private with KMS, you can enable encrypted logs that are only decryptable by your key holder.
[02:52] Ravi: Mechanism — does that mean logs come down encrypted and then we decrypt locally?
[02:56] Samir: Exactly. We store encrypted blobs in the control plane; when you pull them, the control plane streams encrypted blobs to your VPC connector which then requests a decrypt from your KMS. Logs never appear plaintext in our multi-tenant control plane.
[03:12] [03:15] (brief pause)
[03:20] Maya: Walkthrough: here's an error classification panel. We tag errors as 1) model exceptions (OOM, kernel panic), 2) infra exceptions (node preempt, network), 3) policy/rejection (rate limit, auth failure), 4) content-related (policy engine blocked response). Each tag includes heuristics and linked examples.
[03:36] Lena: Are those heuristics editable? We have custom rejection logic upstream.
[03:40] Maya: Yes you can add custom rules in the console under Diagnostics -> Rules. You can define regexes over logs, threshold-based triggers, or link to external SLOs.
[03:49] Marco: Can we export the rule set? We want to audit changes via git.
[03:54] Maya: Yep — Rules are stored as YAML and there's an Export button; we also have an API to pull/push rule bundles.
[04:01] Ravi: On RBAC, can we limit visibility so Ops can see traces but not prompt contents?
[04:06] Samir: Yes. RBAC roles are fine-grained: you can have "trace-only" which shows timings and stack traces but redacts prompt/response bodies. There's also an "audit" role that can request temporary escalations subject to approval and an audit log entry.
[04:20] [04:25] (keyboard noise)
[04:28] Maya: Switching to multi-request correlation. This is useful when a user request fans out to multiple model calls — we stitch by parent-request id and show a waterfall.
[04:36] Lena: In our app we do a routing layer that splits a query into retrieval + generate. Will you show both?
[04:41] Maya: Yes. If the calls go through the Redwood gateway they'll be stitched. If your retrieval step happens outside and you only send prompts in, you'll see only the generate leg. We recommend passing the retrieval ID in an X-Parent header to keep it correlative.
[04:57] Marco: If we have partial failures in the retrieval leg, can the console show those external calls?
[05:02] Maya: We can ingest external spans via our SDK or OTLP and stitch them. We don't automatically scrape your internal services unless you push spans.
[05:10] Ravi: Performance: we need to understand tail latency contributors. Does the console surface percentiles and buffer occupancy?
[05:16] Maya: Yes, the per-route dashboard shows p50/p90/p99 for token latency, queue times, and also per-batch size histograms. You can filter by model version and quantization profile.
[05:28] [05:30] (brief cross talk)
[05:35] Lena: About cost: we have teams worried that enabling request logging with full payloads will blow up retention costs. How do you balance trace fidelity and cost?
[05:44] Samir: Good point. We have configurable retention tiers: traces (headers + timings) at default retention, full payload captures as an optional pruneable artifact. We recommend sampling 1% of full payloads for long-term retention and 100% lightweight timing data. Optimize can suggest sampling rates based on observed error rates.
[06:02] Maya: Also you can enable on-demand capture — e.g., if an alert triggers, the system can flip to "capture-full" for the next 5 minutes for that route.
[06:10] Marco: Nice. Can we run rule-based automated captures?
[06:13] Maya: Yes that's under Diagnostics -> Capture Policies.
[06:17] [06:20] Ravi: Security question — SSO/SAML across regions — we need region-local auth. Does Redwood have regional control plane partitions?
[06:27] Samir: For Private and Dedicated we can deploy a control plane regionally; hosted has data residency options per region and we can route auth to a local IdP via SAML. There are a few caveats around global RBAC sync which we can design around.
[06:40] [06:45] (phone vibration)
[06:47] Maya: I'm going to demo a real trace with an error. Here's a request where the model returned partial output and then a runtime exception. You can see the traceback — sometimes it's an OOM in a custom kernel. In the UI we link to kernel logs and recommend immediate mitigations: reduce max tokens, switch quantization profile, or route to a larger variant.
[07:07] Lena: Do you expose the internal scheduling decisions? We saw some pressure from burst traffic and want to know which layer queued requests.
[07:13] Maya: The timeline shows both gateway queue and executor queue. For Dedicated you also get per-GPU queue depth. We annotate queue waits with a causation tag if it was due to batching or backpressure.
[07:26] Ravi: You mentioned automatic fallback to variants — is that configurable per route?
[07:30] Samir: Yes, per-route policies let you set fallback order, allowed latency delta, and a cost cap. You can also set canary rules — e.g., 5% traffic to a new quantized variant.
[07:42] [07:45] (murmur)
[07:48] Maya: Now, for the incident you described earlier that still returned 500s after fallback — looking at this example trace I can see the fallback succeeded but the downstream postprocessor threw a validation error. That validation happens in your app layer; the console shows a cross-service error with the external status code.
[08:03] Marco: So we need to forward those external status codes into the trace for easier triage?
[08:08] Maya: Exactly. We recommend a convention: include an X-Status header on downstream responses. If you propagate x-request-id it all stitches nicely.
[08:17] Lena: About the sandbox Maya, can you demo the policy that escalates to capture when p99 latency crosses a threshold?
[08:23] Maya: Sure. Here under Capture Policies I have a rule: if route.my-app p99 > 1200ms for two consecutive 5m windows, set capture-full=on for 10 minutes and notify the #ops channel.
[08:36] [08:40] (typing)
[08:42] Maya: I can edit it live — see, change the window to 3m and the capture window to 15m. Save and it's versioned in the rule history.
[08:52] Ravi: Versioned history is great. We need an audit trail for who changed the rule.
[08:56] Samir: All changes are logged and tied to the SSO identity — there's also an approval workflow for sensitive rule edits.
[09:04] Marco: What's the latency impact of the instrumentation? We want minimal overhead.
[09:09] Maya: Lightweight timing headers add ~150-250 microseconds. Full payload capture adds IO cost — if you're streaming to an external store you'll see more. We recommend asynchronous streaming to a buffered write path to avoid affecting p99.
[09:23] Lena: For the pilot, we want to run 48 hours of production traces against your sandbox to see how Console surfaces our issues. Is that possible?
[09:30] Samir: Yes. We can accept traces via OTLP or by uploading a gzipped bundle. For security we'll provision a dedicated tenant with ingress restricted to your IPs and an encrypted storage bucket.
[09:41] Maya: Note: if you upload trace IDs we can automatically link them to our model catalog and infer likely causes using our heuristics engine. That speeds up onboarding.
[09:50] [09:55] (crosstalk)
[09:57] Marco: On the billing side, curious about unit economics on heavy capture. How do you charge for captured payloads?
[10:03] Samir: For hosted we charge based on bytes stored and query units. For Dedicated we have included telemetry tiers in the contract; extra ingestion is billable. We'll provide an estimate based on your sample data.
[10:15] Ravi: Can we limit export so only audit team can export payloads?
[10:19] Maya: Yes that's another RBAC permission — export vs view. Export operations also trigger an audit entry and optional email approvals.
[10:29] [10:30] (pause)
[10:32] Maya: I'm going to show the Failure Mode Explorer. This clusters similar failures by signature. Helpful when you have many 500s but only a few distinct root causes.
[10:43] Lena: Heuristics there often miscluster — can we add custom fingerprints?
[10:47] Maya: Yes you can add a custom fingerprint function or regex that normalizes stack traces. We also allow merging clusters manually and pinning a canonical cause.
[10:56] Marco: For private deployments, do you give us the same UI or an admin-hosted console?
[11:01] Samir: Same UI; for Private the console can be deployed behind your VPC and the control plane runs either in-region or on-prem depending on the package. We still ship updates but you control deployment windows.
[11:12] [11:15] (laptop fan)
[11:18] Maya: Next I'll demo a live trace ingestion. Uploading a small gz bundle now — bear with me.
[11:27] [11:30] (upload progress)
[11:33] Maya: Ingest done. The system parsed 12k spans and linked 712 requests. See how it surfaces an emergent cluster: "policy rejection + downstream timeout". Clicking shows the top sample traces.
[11:46] Ravi: Those spans show an external 504 from our cache layer. Looks familiar.
[11:50] Maya: Right — the console suggests mitigation: increase the cache TTL for that route and add a retry wrapper for transient 504s, or tune the retry to be backoff rather than immediate. It also shows the historical rate of those 504s so you can evaluate impact.
[12:05] Lena: Can we export those sample traces to our SRE tooling?
[12:08] Maya: Yes — Export -> OTLP or raw JSON. We can push to a configured endpoint. Exports can be signed and encrypted.
[12:17] Marco: Anything for proactive detection of model regression, like quality drops?
[12:21] Maya: Optimize integrates with Evals — you can tie prompt sets to routes and get alerts on quality regressions. The console shows QA metrics side-by-side with latency/cost so you can make tradeoffs.
[12:34] Samir: We have a demo notebook for that; I'll attach it after the call.
[12:38] [12:40] (typing)
[12:42] Ravi: Ok, going deeper — if a request is retried multiple times and eventually succeeds, do you collapse them or show them as separate?
[12:49] Maya: You can view both. By default we show a collapsed trace with a retry count and ability to expand each attempt with its timings and responses. This helps to spot transient failures vs persistent ones.
[12:59] Lena: For postmortems we want exportable timelines. Is there a PPT export?
[13:04] Maya: Yes — there's an "Export Incident" which packages the timeline, top traces, screenshots, and a markdown summary you can drop into your postmortem tool.
[13:15] [13:20] (background noise)
[13:22] Marco: Walk me through a hypothetical runbook for a recurring 500 error that suggests root cause is model memory pressure.
[13:28] Maya: The UI suggests runbook steps: 1) Identify the model and version; 2) Check batch sizes and queue wait; 3) If OOM signature, reduce max tokens or move to quantized variant or larger instance; 4) If fallback happened, inspect downstream processors for validation errors; 5) Create a capture and schedule a canary. Each step links to console actions.
[13:50] Ravi: Can we programmatically trigger the canary?
[13:53] Samir: Yes via the API you can flip traffic weights for canaries or trigger an immediate canary run.
[13:59] Lena: About capturing PII — we need to ensure that any PII is redacted at capture time, not just in the UI.
[14:07] Maya: We support client-side redaction hooks where your SDK scrubs PII before sending; server-side we apply redaction rules during ingestion and keep an encrypted redaction key. We can also provide sample regexes used by other customers for common PII patterns.
[14:23] [14:25] (soft chuckle)
[14:27] Marco: Any gotchas to be aware of when stitching traces across multiple clouds? We have part of infra in GCP and part in AWS.
[14:34] Maya: Time skew and header forwarding are the common issues. Ensure NTP sync and consistent x-request-id propagation. We recommend using OTLP with trace id preservation.
[14:45] Ravi: For the pilot, do we need to whitelist IPs for the sandbox?
[14:48] Samir: Yes we'll ask for the minimal CIDR list. We'll provide a guide with steps.
[14:55] Maya: A few more notes: fallback policies can be annotated with estimated cost delta so you can choose to trade latency for unit cost or vice versa. Optimize can run a simulation on your trace sample to estimate cost impact of switching policies.
[15:12] [15:15] (keyboard)
[15:18] Lena: That simulation would be useful — could we get a headcount estimate for the pilot operations?
[15:23] Samir: Typically a 2-3 person engagement for the first week: one SE, one engineering point-of-contact, and one SRE/infra contact. We'll scope exact hours after we see the trace sample.
[15:35] Marco: Security review — we need the SOC2 and data flow diagram before legal signs off.
[15:41] Samir: I'll attach the SOC2, network diagram, and the KMS integration guide. We'll also add the regional control plane notes.
[15:49] [15:50] (brief pause)
[15:53] Ravi: One more technical: when a request is split into multiple tokens batches, does the trace show per-token timing?
[15:59] Maya: We show per-batch timing and an aggregate token breakdown. Per-token can be noisy and expensive to store; we keep it as optional capture for high-fidelity sampling.
[16:12] Lena: Cool. Any limitations for on-prem private deployments?
[16:16] Samir: Resource scheduling must meet GPU driver compatibility; we provide a compatibility matrix. Also some telemetry features require outbound connectivity for updates unless you take a fully air-gapped package.
[16:29] [16:30] (murmur)
[16:32] Maya: Wrapping with a quick recap: we'll provision sandbox, they upload 48h sample traces, we'll run an Optimize sim, and then schedule a 30m pilot kickoff.
[16:44] Marco: Sounds good. Timeline — we want pilot in the week of July 7.
[16:49] Samir: We'll target that. I'll send invites and the security pack. Maya will provision the tenant.
[16:56] Lena: I'll circulate the sample trace export steps and confirm IPs.
[17:00] [17:02] (end of meeting)
[17:03] Samir: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and a quick checklist.
[17:06] Ravi: Thanks.
[17:08] Maya: Bye!

Note: Transcript contains some transcription artifacts (e.g., "CT O" for CTO, "K V cache" in a few spots). Speaker labels are approximated per Fireflies export.
